title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
Before anything: three hands-up questions

Roughly what sets the Earth’s average temperature? (could you explain it to a friend?)
Have you written Python this year?
Do you remember what “climate sensitivity” means?


Ungraded diagnostic — you watched GR5001, they took it a year ago. Watch the hands: this calibrates how much refresher weeks 2–9 need. No judgment framing: “a year is a long time; that’s expected and fine.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: Every number on this figure came out of a model
text:
Every number on this figure came out of a model


The hook. Let it sit. “Sea level in 2100, warming under net-zero, monsoon shifts — every quantitative claim about the climate future is a model output. This course is about whether — and when, and how much — to believe them.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: The question someone is already thinking
text:
The question someone is already thinking

“Aren’t these models just tuned to give the answer the modelers expect?”


This is a real question, asked inside the field too.
November 12 — a full session on tuning, evaluation, and why matching the past doesn’t guarantee the future.
By December you’ll answer it better than most working scientists.

Raise it proactively — trust move. Don’t answer it now beyond one sentence: “the short version is: tuning is real, documented, and much narrower than the accusation implies — the long version needs the machinery we’ll build first.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
What this course is
Last year, GR5001 taught you what the climate system does — and how to interpret climate information.
This course opens the machine that produces that information:

Build the model hierarchy yourselves (in Python)
Understand how the real Earth System Models work
Analyze their output the way practicing scientists do (CMIP6)
Judge what models can and cannot tell you


The one-sentence identity: “you know what the climate does; now, how we know what it will do.” Callbacks to GR5001 will happen every single week — most concepts get rebuilt, properly, with math and code. A year of decay is assumed and fine (Mingfang agrees).

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
By December, you will have

built working models: energy balance → feedbacks → carbon → transient warming
run experiments on them (broken them, fixed them, tuned them)
pulled real CMIP6 output from the cloud and made defensible figures
completed a research project answering a climate question you chose
an informed answer to “should I trust this model result?”


Concrete deliverables, incl. the portfolio value: the final project is a reproducible notebook they can show employers.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
The ladder we’ll climb

Every rung still in active use. The ladder is the course map — today we climb it historically.

Key framing: not a ladder of progress where the top makes the bottom obsolete — a ladder where every rung has a permanent job. Today: meet each rung through the people and problems that created it.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: 1896: Arrhenius computes the climate by hand
text:
1896: Arrhenius computes the climate by hand


Motivated by ice ages, not fossil fuels
Months of hand calculation: radiative budget + water-vapor amplification
His answer for CO₂ doubling: ~5–6 °C (modern: 2.5–4 °C)
The structure of the calculation is recognizably modern


Story beats: Langley’s infrared measurements as data; Arrhenius working through a difficult personal period; got the structure right, the number high. In 1908 he thought warming would take millennia and might be nice — why nobody panicked. 1938 Callendar: one sentence — linked rising CO₂ to observed warming from weather stations, was politely dismissed.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
What Arrhenius’s model was
\[\text{absorbed sunlight} = \text{emitted infrared}\]
One equation. One perturbation (CO₂). One answer (a temperature).

Weeks 2–3: you build exactly this — then make it tick in time, grow an ice cap, and misbehave.

Point at the ladder: rung 1 never retired. FaIR-type models running IPCC scenario numbers today are direct descendants. (Don’t say FaIR yet — “the models the IPCC uses to score policy scenarios.”)

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
1922: Richardson’s magnificent failure


Hand-integrated the fluid equations for a 6-hour forecast over Europe
Result: pressure change of ~145 hPa — absurdly, spectacularly wrong
But the method — grid + finite differences + timestepping — is exactly what every model does today


Why it failed: unfiltered gravity-wave noise in the initial conditions (don’t dwell — “his equations were too honest; they amplified noisy data”). The forecast-factory image: 64,000 human computers with a conductor — it’s literally a parallel supercomputer, 80 years early. Callback in week 5.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: Weather vs climate — the distinction that saves us
text:
Weather vs climate — the distinction that saves us
Weather forecast = initial-value problem — where does this trajectory go? Chaos (Lorenz) kills it beyond ~2 weeks.
Climate projection = boundary-value problem — how do the statistics shift when you push the system?


Casino analogy: no one can predict the next hand. The house margin is a certainty.


THE misconception-killer of week 1 — students will hear “chaos means you can’t predict 2100” forever. GR5001 gave them weather-vs-climate qualitatively; this is the mathematical version. Lorenz: predictability of the first vs second kind.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: 1950: ENIAC, and a lesson in modeling
text:
1950: ENIAC, and a lesson in modeling
Charney, Fjørtoft & von Neumann: the first numerical weather forecast.
Their winning move: simplify — filter Richardson’s equations down to one level of quasi-geostrophic flow.

Progress came from a smarter simple model, not a bigger computer.

The course’s thesis in one anecdote. The 24-hour forecast took ~24 hours of ENIAC time — “keeping pace with the weather.” This moral repeats: Stommel (wk 4), the EBMs, FaIR.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
1967: Manabe & Wetherald


1-D radiative-convective column: real spectroscopy + convection pinning the lapse rate
CO₂ doubling → ECS ≈ 2.3 °C — within today’s assessed range
2015 poll of climate scientists: the most influential climate-change paper ever


Suki Manabe: arrived from Tokyo 1958, GFDL. The insight: get one column right before doing the sphere. Fig. 16’s quiet bombshell — stratospheric cooling while the surface warms: a fingerprint prediction, made decades before it was observed, that pure solar warming would NOT produce. Week 2 builds the toy version; week 9 returns for feedbacks.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
1956: Phillips spins up a planet
Two-level model, one hemisphere, a month of simulated time.
Jets and storm tracks appeared — nobody coded them.

This is emergence: put conservation laws on a grid, and the general circulation is what falling into balance looks like.

Phillips’s numerical experiment ran on a machine with ~5KB of memory. Emergence is week 5’s big idea — plant the phrase “you never coded a Hadley cell” now.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
The lineage to today

1969 Manabe & Bryan: first coupled atmosphere–ocean model
1975 Manabe & Wetherald: first 3-D CO₂-doubling experiment → polar amplification predicted
1979 Charney Report: with two GCMs in the world, ECS = 1.5–4.5 °C
2021 AR6: ECS = 2.5–4 °C


42 years to narrow the bar by half. Why so slow? (Hold that thought until Nov 5.)

Plant the week-9 mystery explicitly — it’s the best cliffhanger the field has. Polar amplification: predicted in ’75, now observed at ~4x global rate in the Arctic. Predictions-that-came-true list is the honest counterweight to the tuning question.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
Modeling becomes coordinated science

1988 Hansen testifies to the Senate; 1990 first IPCC report
1995→ CMIP: every modeling center runs the same experiments — models become comparable, and their spread becomes data
Carbon, chemistry, vegetation, ice sheets join → GCMs become Earth System Models
2021 Nobel Prize in Physics: Manabe & Hasselmann


CMIP is Act IV’s subject: the students will use CMIP6 data themselves from HW1 onward (lightly) and deeply from week 11. The Nobel framing: “physics recognized that climate physics is physics.”

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
The frontier (where this course ends)

Km-scale simulation: resolving storms and ocean eddies globally — computationally heroic
AI emulators: neural networks forecasting weather competitively, now creeping into climate
The perpetually unsolved: clouds

Week 13: what’s hype, what’s real.

One slide, no depth — just show the course reaches the present. GraphCast/NeuralGCM-class models by name only if asked.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
Why keep the whole ladder? (Held, 2005)

Climate science needs a hierarchy of models the way biology needs model organisms.


Simulation ≠ understanding — you can simulate what you don’t understand
A gap between them is dangerous: you can’t tell trustworthy projections from artifacts
Simple models are where understanding lives — and they discover things (a 1961 two-box model found a possible AMOC collapse before any GCM could)


Held’s essay is the intellectual backbone of the course design — say so. The Stommel teaser sets up week 4. If anyone wants one reading from today: this one, it’s short and equation-free.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text:
Fit for purpose
“Which model is best?” is meaningless without “…for what question?”







Question
Right tool




Why is there a greenhouse effect?
pencil + 0-D EBM


Will this El Niño bring drought?
initialized coupled GCM


Warming in 2100 under scenario X?
ESM ensemble + simple-model emulator


Could the AMOC collapse?
box model (mechanism) + ESM (when/whether)




Note the last row deliberately has TWO answers — mechanism rung + projection rung. That’s the segue to the activity, where several questions do too.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
section: Your turn — match the question to the rung (15 min)
text:
Your turn — match the question to the rung (15 min)
In pairs: the handout lists 6 climate questions and the model hierarchy.

For each question: which rung(s)? One minute of gut feeling, then argue.
Write your matches + one sentence of justification each
Names on the slip, hand it in (counts toward participation)


Deliberately light. Circulate, listen. Debrief (5 min): call out that half the questions have two defensible answers — mechanism vs projection — and that noticing this IS the learning objective. Cuttable on the day if running long.

title: Lab 0 — Getting Set Up
text:
Due: before class on Thursday, September 24 (Lab 1 happens in class that day and assumes all of this works). Time needed: ~30–45 minutes. Do it this week — if anything fails, come to office hours or email the TAs before Sep 24, not the night before.
By the end of this lab you will have: (1) a working JupyterHub login, (2) a GitHub account with a private course repository shared with the teaching staff, and (3) one completed notebook pushed to that repository and linked on Courseworks. This is the exact workflow you’ll use to submit every lab and homework this semester.

title: Lab 0 — Getting Set Up
text:
Part A — Accounts (10 min)

GitHub. If you don’t have an account, create one at github.com/signup. Use a professional-ish username (it may end up on your CV — many of you will link to course projects later). Enable two-factor authentication (GitHub requires it).
JupyterHub. You will receive an invitation to the course computing hub at [HUB-URL — to be announced on Courseworks]. Log in with the credentials from the invite and confirm your server starts (click “Start My Server” and wait for the JupyterLab interface to load).


If the hub won’t start for you: email the TAs with a screenshot. As a backup, every course notebook also runs on Google Colab — but sort out your hub access this week regardless; we’ll need it for the second half of the course.

title: Lab 0 — Getting Set Up
section: Part B — Run the verification notebook (10 min)
text:
Part B — Run the verification notebook (10 min)

Download verify_setup.ipynb from the Courseworks Lab 0 assignment page.
On the hub: drag-and-drop the file into the JupyterLab file browser (left panel).
Open it and run every cell (Shift+Enter, or Run ▸ Run All Cells).

title: Lab 0 — Getting Set Up
section: Part C — Create your course repository (15 min)
text:
Part C — Create your course repository (15 min)

On GitHub, click New repository:

Name: climate-modeling-f26-<your-uni> (e.g., climate-modeling-f26-ab1234)
Visibility: Private ← important
Check “Add a README file”

Add the teaching staff as collaborators: repo Settings → Collaborators → Add people — add [INSTRUCTOR-GITHUB], [PRANI-GITHUB], and [CHANDANIE-GITHUB].
Put your completed notebook in the repo. Two ways — pick one:

Easy way (fine for today): on your repo’s GitHub page, Add file → Upload files, drag in the completed verify_setup.ipynb (download it from the hub first: right-click the file → Download), and click Commit changes.
Real way (we’ll all use this from Lab 1 on): in a hub Terminal (File → New → Terminal):
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/climate-modeling-f26-<uni>.git
cp verify_setup.ipynb climate-modeling-f26-<uni>/
cd climate-modeling-f26-<uni>
git add verify_setup.ipynb
git commit -m "Lab 0: verification notebook"
git push
GitHub will ask you to authenticate — you’ll need a personal access token instead of your password: GitHub Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) → Generate new token (scope: repo; set expiration to end of December). Paste the token when git push asks for a password. Save it somewhere — you’ll reuse it all semester.

title: Introduction to Climate Modeling
text: Earth system and climate models are critically important tools for climate science — used to study past climate variability, attribute recent trends and extremes, and project the evolution of the climate system under natural and anthropogenic forcing. This course opens the machine: you will build the hierarchy of climate models yourself in Python, understand how full Earth System Models work, analyze their output (CMIP6) the way practicing scientists do, and learn to judge what models can and cannot tell you.

title: Final Project
text:
You will develop your own research question and answer it using either output from real climate model simulations (CMIP6 and related archives) or experiments with a simple model of the kind built in class — or both. The deliverable is a reproducible Jupyter notebook documenting your analysis and insights, presented in class during the final weeks.
Examples of the format and spirit: Earth & Environmental Data Science project gallery.
